title: 3-to-9 arpeggios over the major 7th chords

review.reviewedBy: Claude, the AI that wrote it

inspiration.note: Kessel often built lines from arpeggios placed over a chord rather than on its root, such as a major 7th arpeggio started on the 3rd of a minor 7th chord (a 3-to-9 arpeggio). This phrase applies the same idea to two major 7th chords: a minor 7th arpeggio started on the 3rd of each.

sources.detail: Jazz Guitar Online lesson. Lick 9 uses the '3-9 arpeggio' (a major 7th arpeggio from the 3rd of a minor 7th chord), and licks 6 and 7 show other arpeggios Kessel placed over a chord, such as a minor 7th arpeggio over a dominant 7th.

analysis.summary: Each major 7th chord gets the minor 7th arpeggio that starts on its 3rd. Over {{chord 1}} that shape climbs through the 3rd, 5th and 7th to the 9th, {{note 1.5}}; over {{chord 2}} the same shape, now built on that chord's 3rd, runs down from {{note 2.1}} and turns back up. Half steps connect the pieces, and the line lands on the b3 of {{chord 3}} on beat one, where the tune's minor ii–V begins.

points.text: {{note 1.2}}, {{note 1.3}} and {{note 1.4}} are the 3rd, 5th and 7th of {{chord 1}}; {{note 2.1}}, {{note 2.3}} and {{note 2.4}} are the 3rd, 7th and 5th of {{chord 2}}. Neither arpeggio plays the root. The bass already has it, so the line can stay on the notes that give each chord its colour.

{{note 1.5}} is the 9th of {{chord 1}} and {{note 2.2}} is the 9th of {{chord 2}}. Stack each arpeggio in 3rds from the 3rd and the 9th is simply its fourth note, so the extension comes for free. On a major 7th chord the 9th is a smooth, consonant colour, which is why it can sit on beat three of bar 1.

{{note 1.8}} sits a half step below {{note 2.1}} and pushes into the 3rd of {{chord 2}} right on the bar line. {{note 2.8}} is a chromatic passing note: it walks the 7th of {{chord 2}} down by half steps into the b3 of {{chord 3}}.

The line starts on the 'and' of beat one, just after the downbeat, so the first arpeggio pushes up towards the 9th on beat three. In bar 2 every beat carries a guide tone of {{chord 2}}: 3rd, 7th, 3rd, 7th, with the 9th, the 5th and one passing note on the off-beats. The landing note falls on beat one and is held for two beats.

{{note 3.1}} is the b3 of {{chord 3}}, reached by half steps from the 7th of {{chord 2}}. It is also the 7th of the dominant chord that comes next in the tune, so it carries straight on into the minor ii–V.

whyItWorks: Start a minor 7th arpeggio on the 3rd of a major 7th chord and you get the chord's 3rd, 5th and 7th plus its 9th: all of its colour without the root, which the bass already plays. A shape you already know gives you a richer sound. Half steps link each shape to the next chord, so the line never loses the harmony.
fingeringNote: One position throughout, with no stretches or shifts: as written, the index finger covers fret 5 and nothing goes past fret 8. The third finger starts the line on the G string, and the first arpeggio climbs across the strings to the high E string, where the index and little fingers take the 7th and 9th. In bar 2 the shape walks down to the D string, with the little finger on the 5th of {{chord 2}}; the closing half steps on the G string use fingers 3, 2 and 1.
practiceTask: Play it over bars 3 to 5 of the weekly standard, then over bars 11 to 13 and 23 to 25, where the same three chords come back. Then improvise a chorus in which every major 7th chord in the tune gets only the minor 7th arpeggio built on its 3rd.

variation.description: Same two arpeggios, new target. At the end of bar 2 the line climbs instead of falling, so the 7th of {{chord 2}} rises a half step to {{note 3.1}}, the b5 of {{chord 3}}: the note that makes the chord half-diminished.
